# Why Architecture Work Is Getting Harder {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"[F]eedback is the control of a system by reinserting into the system the results of its performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."*
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings* (1950) [@Wiener1950HumanUse, p. 71]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Norbert Wiener, who helped establish cybernetics, made feedback the defining property of control. In the passage quoted, he separates feedback that merely regulates a system from feedback that changes how the system acts. Architecture work turns on the same distinction, and this chapter is about what happens when the regulating kind stops being enough.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
Why does modern architecture work demand new forms of assistance, and where can
that assistance help without weakening the comparison?

:::

Architecture work is getting harder, not because good ideas are scarcer but
because each design must hold more of the system at once. Parameters across
microarchitecture, power delivery, packaging, and software interact in ways
that no single model or heuristic covers. A cache-sizing decision, for example,
can change software latency, memory traffic, die area, and package-level power.

Architecture teams repeatedly frame questions, propose candidates, evaluate
them with workloads and tools, and revise them in light of the results. A
modern architecture study spans more design information, more software and physical
constraints, more possible designs, and more expensive forms of evaluation
than an earlier one. It must keep those elements consistent long enough to
support a decision. Much of the performance and efficiency that once arrived
with the next process node must now be found through architecture,
specialization, software, and system composition.

This is not a flat list of independent problems. Microarchitecture and
multicore execution add policies and coherence. Specialization tailors a block
to a workload. Composing specialized blocks into a system-on-chip (SoC), a
chiplet-based system, or a warehouse-scale computer adds integration
boundaries. Compilers, runtimes, libraries, and applications keep changing
while the hardware is being designed. Physical and verification checks become
more consequential just as they become more expensive.

The result is a compounding problem. A specialized hardware choice changes the
software path needed to use it. That software path changes the workload and
data movement seen by the hardware. Physical limits can then reverse a ranking
that looked favorable in an early model, and verification must cover the new
interfaces and behaviors that the choice introduced. A fair comparison must
therefore carry more of the complete system.

Historically, architects have answered comparable increases in complexity by
raising the level of abstraction and making important interfaces, rules, and
measurements explicit. Instruction set architectures, hardware description
languages, logic synthesis, shared benchmarks, and programming models each
allowed people and tools to work on a larger system without reasoning about
every transistor. Artificial intelligence (AI) may increase design capacity in
the same spirit, but only when it addresses work that has become limiting.
Generating more candidates is not progress when simulation, verification, or
expert review cannot keep pace.

Architecture has faced widening complexity before. Its earlier responses show
what a useful new form of assistance must preserve even when the scale and
coupling of the design problem change.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Trace how microarchitecture, specialization, composition, software change,
  physical limits, evaluation cost, and verification compound inside one
  architecture comparison.
- Explain why the changing technology dividend has shifted more responsibility to
  architecture, specialization, software, and system composition.
- Distinguish the size of a design space from the cost and strength of the
  evaluations needed to compare it.
- Diagnose where AI assistance might help and identify the executable software,
  physical, and verification checks that must remain authoritative.

:::

## How Architecture Has Absorbed Complexity

Before asking where new assistance might help, it is useful to examine how
architecture has handled earlier increases in complexity. The field has
repeatedly raised the level at which engineers describe a design and made
interfaces, rules, tool paths, and comparisons explicit. The gain is not that
constraints disappear. People and tools can work on larger design objects
while lower-level checks still reject choices that fail in implementation.

Architecture work has always moved through repeated cycles of analysis and
revision. A typical study begins with an aim such as improving latency,
reducing energy, raising throughput, supporting a workload, or fitting a system
within a power and cost envelope. The architect chooses an abstraction, builds
or selects a model, runs an analysis or simulation, studies the result, and
revises the design so that surviving work eventually reaches implementation,
validation, verification, and signoff. Textbooks and industrial practice both
follow this basic pattern.

Consider a traditional Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation (SPEC) CPU
study. An architect selects workloads, proposes a cache-hierarchy or
branch-predictor change, runs a simulator or performance model, and inspects
instructions per cycle (IPC), miss rates, branch-misprediction rates, and area
and power estimates. Candidates that help one workload while harming others may
be revised or discarded. Human judgment shapes the comparison throughout, from
workload selection and proxy choice to the decision that a candidate deserves
deeper analysis.

SPEC CPU 2017 provides an industry-standard suite for compute-intensive
performance across processor, memory-system, and compiler behavior
[@SPEC2017CPU]. What matters here is how the comparison is bounded. Its
workloads, run rules, and reporting conventions make candidates easier to
compare under stated conditions.

What makes that comparison sound is not all written into it. Experienced
architects carry the rest implicitly. They know which workloads were excluded,
which tool settings are trusted, why a previous candidate failed, and what
decision is actually under review. As design programs scale, keeping that context
synchronized across larger teams and more complex toolchains becomes harder and
can limit progress.

Turning implicit knowledge into an inspectable artifact is not a new demand.
Architects have repeatedly changed their working methods when informal
coordination stopped being sufficient. Some changes stabilized an interface.
Others established shared design rules, benchmarks, tool paths, or criteria
for rejecting a candidate. Each shift made a different part of the design work
explicit (@tbl-historical-loop-transformations). These shifts did not each
invent the practice named in the table. They made a consequential part of the
work explicit enough to share, check, or automate. Across the examples, the
recurring move was to expose a contract, representation, tool path, or
comparison that could coordinate a larger design effort.

| **Shift** | **What the design process made explicit** | **Why it mattered** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System/360 compatibility | A stable Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) contract separated architecture from implementation across a product family [@AmdahlBlaauwBrooks1964System360]. | The ISA carries architectural commitments across implementations and product generations. |
| Mead--Conway VLSI and MOSIS | Design rules, layout abstractions, and fabrication access turned custom-chip design into a shareable and reusable loop [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @USCISI2025MOSISFirstYear]. | Shared representations and fabrication access broaden participation in architecture work. |
| Reduced instruction set computer (RISC) | The RISC argument linked ISA choices to compiler behavior, Very Large-Scale Integration (VLSI) implementation, workloads, and quantitative cost/performance [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. | A complete comparison includes the workload, compiler, and implementation cost. |
| SPEC-style benchmarking | Workload selection, run rules, reporting conventions, and comparability became community infrastructure [@SPEC2017CPU]. | Benchmarks govern workload choice, execution, and comparison. |
| Logic synthesis and timing closure | Hardware Description Language (HDL), libraries, constraints, and timing reports let downstream checks reject upstream choices [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization]. | Implementation checks can rule out architecture candidates before the design team commits to them. |
| CUDA-style graphics processing unit (GPU) programming | Kernels, thread hierarchies, memory spaces, libraries, and toolchains made specialized hardware programmable [@NickollsEtAl2008CUDA]. | Specialized hardware needs a usable programming model and toolchain. |

: **Six changes that made architecture work easier to inspect.** Each one established a shared representation, interface, tool path, benchmark, or decision criterion where informal coordination no longer sufficed. {#tbl-historical-loop-transformations tbl-colwidths="[22,39,28]"}

The examples solve different coordination problems. System/360 and CUDA make
interfaces explicit so that implementations and software can evolve around a
shared contract. Mead--Conway methods and logic synthesis connect a design to
the rules and tools that can accept or reject it. SPEC makes results comparable
across machines, and RISC shows why a hardware claim must include the workload,
compiler, and implementation cost. In each case, progress depended on making
more of the design work visible to other people and tools. Several of these
shifts also raised the level of abstraction so that one engineer's decision
governed more of the design. That is the mechanism by which the discipline has
repeatedly closed a widening gap between what a process can fabricate and what a
team can design, and the measured version of that gap returns in
@sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure once today's version is in view.

Representations and interfaces coordinate what can change independently. A
release strategy can instead allocate when a team takes different technical
risks. Intel's tick-tock model stated one such strategy publicly. A known
microarchitecture moved to a new process in one release, and a new
microarchitecture followed on the now-proven process in the next, so no release
attempted both at once. The rule held only while the process schedule did.

As node transitions lengthened, Intel retired the two-step model and stated
that it would keep each process technology in use longer, adding an optimization
step to the sequence [@Intel2016Form10K]. The schedule changed because the
earlier division of technical risk no longer fit the work. An explicit rule can
be checked against the conditions that justified it and revised when those
conditions move.

These changes did not eliminate iteration. They made the design's information,
choices, measurements, and decisions explicit enough for other people and tools
to work with. High-level synthesis and parameterized hardware generators extend
the same history [@CoussyMorawiec2008HighLevelSynthesis;
@Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. They raise the description above individual
register-transfer level (RTL) structures, but lower-level synthesis, timing,
physical, and verification checks still reject inadequate results. Raising the
level of abstraction scales design work by preserving consequential checks, not
by making those checks unnecessary.

The artifacts do not explain themselves. Architectural knowledge is
distributed across specifications, constraints, scripts, traces, tool versions,
and review decisions. A shared interface or representation helps only when a
team also knows which assumptions are fixed, which choices may change, and which
downstream check can reject a proposal. Modern specialization requires several
of those boundaries to remain consistent at once.

This history supplies a response pattern, not a guarantee that existing
abstractions remain sufficient. Earlier process generations often supplied
broadly reusable gains while new abstractions helped teams manage the added
transistors. More of today's benefit depends on workload-specific architecture,
software, and physical choices. The underlying technology dividend has changed.

## The Technology Dividend Has Changed

The historical shifts above addressed problems of scale and coordination by
making more of the design explicit. The pressure is different today because
process and device technology still supply essential improvements without
automatically delivering the broadly reusable gains architects once expected
from each generation. More of the benefit must now come from choices that bind
architecture, software, and physical implementation together.

### Scaling No Longer Supplies the Same Gains

Process technology remains fundamental, but it no longer automatically converts
density into the same broadly reusable combination of frequency, single-thread
performance, and energy efficiency. For roughly fifty years, processor
generations improved through a familiar progression. Transistor density
continued to rise while
voltage scaling made it possible, for a time, to use more transistors without a
proportional increase in power [@Moore1965Cramming;
@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. Quantitative analysis gave architects a way to compare
the resulting design choices. As voltage and frequency scaling slowed,
microarchitecture, parallelism, and eventually domain specialization carried
more of the burden
[@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach;
@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. Fifty years of frontier microprocessor data
show the resulting divergence. Clock frequency plateaued in the mid-2000s,
while transistor counts continued to rise, hardware-thread counts turned
upward, and the CPU power frontier in the dataset reached hundreds of watts
(@fig-microprocessor-trends).

The diverging curves mark the end of a free lunch
[@Sutter2005FreeLunch]. Transistor counts kept climbing, but once Dennard
scaling ended around 2005, the single-thread gains historically associated
with each generation slowed from roughly 50 percent a year to a few percent
[@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Further gains now had to fit
within the power a package could dissipate.

The power series also needs a careful reading. The value near 300\ W is the
highest entry in the final four-year interval of the public dataset, not a
typical processor thermal design power. Like the other series, it shows the
frontier represented in the dataset so that the directions of change can be
compared on one chart.

Constant-field scaling depended on lowering voltage as transistor dimensions
shrank [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. Once voltage scaling slowed, power limited how
many transistors could operate at full frequency at the same time
[@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon]. That constraint helps explain both the
frequency plateau in @fig-microprocessor-trends and the dark-silicon fraction
that followed, the share of a chip that must remain inactive to fit its power
budget. The discipline responded increasingly with parallelism and
specialization. Those responses handed architects more of the machine to
manage rather than inheriting the benefit from the next process node.

The figure stops with the measured history. It does not establish what comes
next. Technology continues to supply transistors, but it no longer turns those
transistors into proportional frequency or single-thread performance
automatically. Architects must find the benefit through parallelism,
specialization, software, and system structure. The rest of the chapter traces
how those choices enlarge the comparison before asking where assistance might
help.

### Specialization Couples the Stack

Technology, architecture, workloads, compilers, and implementation were never
independent. The RISC history above already made a hardware claim depend on its
workload, compiler, and quantitative implementation cost. The layered stack
remains useful because it separates kinds of reasoning. Device technology
supplies transistor characteristics, architecture organizes the machine, and
the optimization layer covers the mapping, scheduling, and tuning that connect
software to it. Specialization does not create the coupling. It tightens the
coupling, increases the consequences of a mismatch, and makes the joint
comparison harder.

Specialization changes the strength of these relationships rather than the
existence of the relationships themselves (@fig-tao-vs-taos).

![**Specialization tightens existing cross-layer coupling:** An accelerator decision can bind software mapping and scheduling, architecture mechanisms, and technology and physical limits more tightly, increasing the cost of a mismatch and the evidence needed to compare candidates.](images/ch2_tao_vs_taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="100%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. On the left, optimization, architecture, and technology form a vertical analytical stack with technology at the base. On the right, the same three layers are joined to a specialization panel by double-headed arrows, and a red dashed boundary labeled tightly coupled physical constraints encloses the entire stack."}

The layered view keeps optimization, architecture, and technology distinct
enough to reason about separately. The specialization-coupled view retains that
decomposition while making the two-way dependence explicit and enclosing the
choices within shared power, thermal, and area limits. Specialization therefore
makes a workload mapping, architecture mechanism, and physical implementation
more consequential to one another. It does not make a previously independent
stack become coupled.

Leaning harder on caches, speculation, vector units, multicore processors,
accelerators, and system-level optimization recovered efficiency. Every one of
those choices also created a new way for an early model to rank the wrong
candidate. The comparison grows again when those mechanisms become parts of a
larger system.

A larger design space is useful only when architects have the information
needed to compare its choices. That requirement connects the changing
technology dividend to the hardware, software, and evaluation pressures that
follow.

## Hardware Scale, Specialization, and Composition

The places where a comparison gets harder track the growth of what counts as
the computer. Microarchitecture adds policies inside one core, specialization
ties a block to one workload, composition puts many blocks in one package, and
wafer-scale integration extends one fabric across a new physical scale. Each
step multiplies the parameters an architect can set and the interactions a fair
comparison cannot leave out.

### Microarchitecture Adds Interacting Costs and Corner Cases

Start with the levers already in every architect's toolkit. A deeper pipeline, a more aggressive branch predictor, a speculative scheduler, or a larger cache hierarchy each recovers performance. That is the material of microarchitecture.

Each of those levers also adds corner cases a fair comparison must cover. A prefetcher that helps one access pattern can pollute a cache under another. A speculation policy that raises throughput can raise energy, and the same speculative machinery later proved able to leak data across protection boundaries, as Spectre and Meltdown showed [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown]. A gain measured on one workload can carry a cost that surfaces only under another.

That these levers have intrinsic limits is not a recent discovery. Palacharla, Jouppi, and Smith showed that the wakeup, selection, and bypass logic of a wide issue window scales badly enough to bound the clock it can support [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective]. Agarwal and colleagues then projected that wire delay and clock scaling together would end the frequency-first road for conventional microarchitectures [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

These costs are not hypothetical. Intel's Pentium 4, built on the NetBurst
microarchitecture, reached 31 pipeline stages in its 90\ nm Prescott generation
as part of a design that emphasized high clock frequency
[@BoggsEtAl2004Pentium4NinetyNm]. More stages can shorten the work done in one
cycle, but they also increase the refill work after a branch misprediction and
add pipeline overhead. The example makes the tradeoff concrete. Frequency is
not an independent design objective; the mechanism used to raise it changes the
work each instruction requires and the energy the machine expends.

That turn to multiple cores added a further layer. Coherence protocols, memory-ordering rules, synchronization costs, and workload partitioning all shape how a candidate behaves under a real workload, and none of them shows up in a single-thread proxy. Even here, before any specialized block is added, the information a comparison must carry has already outgrown a single number.

### Specialization Widens the Hardware-Software Choice

Specialization is a spectrum rather than a jump from a central processing unit
(CPU) to one kind of accelerator. General-purpose cores can add vector and
matrix instructions, GPUs expose wide parallel execution, domain-specific
accelerators tailor dataflow and memory to a workload class, and fixed-function
application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) remove still more flexibility.
Moving along that spectrum can improve efficiency while narrowing the set of
workloads and software paths the hardware can serve.

The spectrum changes what a comparison must weigh. Microarchitecture and
multicore mechanisms tune a general-purpose machine, while specialization
tailors more of the hardware to a particular workload. That changes both the
metrics that matter and the number of choices the architect must evaluate. A
battery- and thermally limited mobile part and a warehouse-scale system bounded
by power delivery and total cost of ownership (TCO) demand different measures
of efficiency, and a specialized block is only worth judging against one such
target.

The opportunity is large. For the kernels studied by Hameed and colleagues, a
fixed-function ASIC was roughly 500
times more energy efficient than a general-purpose core
[@HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency]. Much of that difference came from eliminating
instruction fetch, decode, and unnecessary data movement, then exploiting wider
parallelism and fused operations. The result does not promise the same gain for
every workload. It shows why choosing what to specialize, what flexibility to
retain, and what software interface to expose has become a central architecture
problem.

Specialization has already produced that range of designs. The authors of
Project Brainwave called the expansion a "Cambrian explosion"
[@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Across power and performance, the resulting parts
form a dense, heterogeneous mix of GPUs, FPGAs, neural processors, and other
specialized designs (@fig-accelerator-landscape).

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The AI-accelerator landscape spans seven orders of magnitude in power.** Each point is a publicly announced accelerator from the MIT Lincoln Laboratory survey [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]: color marks form factor (chip, card, or system), filled versus hollow marks training versus inference, and the dashed diagonals are constant energy-efficiency contours. The "Cambrian explosion" is a dense, heterogeneous cloud rather than a single design point.
#| out-width: "100%"

Dashed diagonal lines mark constant energy efficiency from 100 giga-ops per watt to 100 tera-ops per watt. Chips, cards, and systems are colored distinctly; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    ax.text(2.4e-3, eff * 2.4e-3 * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker="o", facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker="o", facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 1.5, 1.6e2),
                  ("Data-center cards", 4e2, 3.0e6), ("Data-center systems", 6e3, 3.0e7)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label = {d["label"]: d for d in rows}
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
```

Power increases from left to right and peak performance from bottom to top.
The dashed diagonals mark equal operations per watt. Color separates chips,
cards, and full systems, while filled and hollow markers separate training from
inference parts. Across those groups, publicly announced accelerators span seven
orders of magnitude in power and six in performance, with no single operating
point a designer can treat as the target. These peak values do not provide a
common architectural ranking. They use different numerical precisions and
operation definitions and do not report delivered performance on one matched
workload. Each point is a distinct bundle of interfaces and constraints, and
choosing among them is the widened comparison this section is about.

An architect must decide what to specialize, where the specialized function
belongs, and how it communicates with the rest of the system. Choosing between
a central processing unit (CPU) and an accelerator is only the start. The
decision also raises questions about vector length, memory hierarchy, local
buffers, compression, dataflow, precision, runtime scheduling, compiler
support, deadlines, thermal behavior, and fallback modes.

Specialization often moves high-volume computation to a heterogeneous set of
Domain Specific Architectures (DSAs), while general-purpose cores retain control
work and the computation that is not worth specializing. The balance varies by
system rather than following one universal partition. Each new DSA can still add
a programming model, instruction set extension, or toolchain obligation.

Specialization also ties a candidate's worth to one workload's efficiency
measure. Before sizing a specialized block, an architect asks Amdahl's question,
namely what fraction of the deployed workload the block actually covers. If the
targeted kernels account for half the execution time, an accelerator that runs
them ten times faster improves total execution time by at most about 1.8 times,
because the untouched half now dominates [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor].
Specialization's ceiling is set by the work it leaves behind on the
general-purpose core. A specialized block must
therefore be compared together with the compiler, runtime, memory traffic, and
remaining workload that determine its delivered benefit.

### SoC and Chiplet Composition

Specialized blocks rarely ship alone. Architects compose them into a
system-on-chip and, increasingly, across multiple chiplets. Yield is one
important motivation. Under simple random-defect models, the fraction of good
dies falls rapidly as die area and defect density rise, so partitioning a large
die can improve die yield [@Murphy1964CostSize]. It does not make total cost
linear because package technology, chiplet and package reuse, and heterogeneous
process choices change the cost model
[@FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. Chiplets also let architects mix process
technologies, intellectual property (IP) blocks, and memory. Open
standards such as UCIe stabilize the interface while leaving partitioning and
implementation to architects [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec].

Composition adds a dense layer of coupled choices in return. A chiplet system is
more than a larger board-level system inside a package. The package alters
latency, bandwidth, energy, thermal coupling, and physical constraints. A modern
SoC also integrates heterogeneous IP blocks, often from different vendors.

Real SoCs are often brownfield systems. An architect may have to integrate a new
accelerator with legacy controllers and proprietary physical-interface blocks
whose vendor does not provide the source RTL. Undocumented interface behavior,
mismatched reset sequences, and clock-domain crossing (CDC) constraints resist
analytical modeling. Coherence-protocol mismatches [@Arm2020AXI] and unstated
timing constraints can emerge when the full SoC is assembled. NoC routing can
also deadlock when its channel-dependency graph contains a cycle.
[^fn-soc-deadlocks-c02] Such problems may remain latent until integration-level
verification or bring-up.

Each added block narrows the set of valid designs. Moving a function across a
chiplet boundary changes the available interfaces, software path, and tools
needed to evaluate it.

This composition challenge extends directly to routing congestion. A
network-on-chip (NoC) may have to arbitrate between bursty accelerator traffic
and a real-time client with a fixed deadline. Average bandwidth can look
adequate while contention still violates the deadline.

[^fn-soc-deadlocks-c02]: **Routing deadlocks**: A routing function is deadlock-free when its channel-dependency graph has no cycles. Virtual channels can remove those cycles [@DallySeitz1987DeadlockFree].

The search can fail in two opposite ways. If its choices are broad but poorly
constrained, it spends evaluations on combinations that cannot be implemented.
If its choices are too narrow, it may search efficiently while excluding the
change needed to satisfy the task. Before the search begins, the architect
needs to state which transformations are permitted, which interfaces are
fixed, what makes a combination valid, and how much reliable evaluation is
available. Candidate count alone answers none of those questions.

Across a multi-vendor package, some of those answers do not exist to be stated.
The Semiconductor Research Corporation's Microelectronics and Advanced
Packaging Technologies (MAPT) roadmap argues that design automation for
packaged multi-vendor systems is blocked by the absence of standard data
formats, syntax, and semantics across suppliers, on the grounds that a
non-process cannot be automated
[@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. An optimizer cannot check an
integration rule that no supplier has written down in a form it can read.

Composition multiplies the physical and economic constraints a candidate must
satisfy, and each one adds evaluation the search cannot skip. Long software
bring-up workloads can exceed the practical reach of detailed software
simulation, so teams may move to hardware emulation or field-programmable gate
array (FPGA) prototyping. FireSim provides one concrete FPGA-accelerated
simulation design point [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Each platform makes its
own tradeoff among execution throughput, observability, hardware, and setup
effort.

Chiplet manufacturing, security, power integrity, and IP interfaces each
require an independent check. In 2.5D and 3D integration such as TSMC CoWoS
[@TSMCCoWoS] or Intel Foveros [@IntelFoveros], discovering a defective die after
packaging can waste other components in the assembly. Pre-bond screening
reduces that risk without proving that every die will survive assembly and
operation, so a proposed partition must preserve adequate test access and
support pre-bond screening that can establish Known-Good-Die
status.[^fn-known-good-die-c02]

[^fn-known-good-die-c02]: **Known-Good-Die (KGD)**: KGD is the screening status assigned to a bare die judged suitable for assembly. Test-access work for three-dimensional stacks covers both pre-stacking die tests and post-stacking tests because screening one die does not establish the behavior of the completed assembly [@MarinissenEtAl2010PrePostBond; @IEEE2020Std1838].

Sharing speculative-state buffers or execution units across secure and
non-secure domains can save power while
opening side channels, so security must be checked by formal methods or
penetration testing that performance proxies cannot stand in for. Supplying
substantial current through a dense package produces voltage loss across the
power network, commonly called IR drop, and localized
hotspots, so a power delivery network (PDN) and thermomechanical model, not an
aggregate-power proxy, decides whether a layout passes signoff. Much of the SoC
is opaque as well. Official product documentation illustrates the range. Arm
has offered processor IP as a process-specific hard macro
[@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro], while Intel documents encrypted RTL whose permitted
uses can be controlled by a generated license [@Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP]. In
either case, an architecture study may
have less access to the block's internals than to an in-house design, which
raises the importance of integration-level testing at its interfaces.

### Wafer-Scale Systems

Some systems need more compute, memory capacity, or bandwidth than one
conventional package can provide within the intended power envelope.
Wafer-scale integration extends the machine to a new physical scale while
retaining one tightly coupled fabric [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. Large
machine-learning accelerators make this pressure especially visible, but the
architecture tradeoff is not limited to AI workloads.

Keeping many compute and memory regions on one wafer-scale fabric can reduce
communication overhead relative to a board- or rack-scale path. It also brings
power delivery, physical reach, manufacturing yield, routing, repair, thread
scheduling, and data placement into the same architecture comparison. In one
wafer-scale GPU study, physical constraints
reduced a nominal capacity of about 100 GPU modules to roughly 40, and the
authors had to co-design scheduling and data placement with the hardware
[@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU].

Wafer scale therefore exposes concerns that otherwise appear across the path
from package to rack. Faulty dies or links may require redundancy and
rerouting, while communication distance and software placement determine how
much of the fabric is useful. A comparison that counts only peak compute can
miss the power-delivery area, communication, repair, and mapping choices that
determine usable capacity.

At each physical scale, the delivered benefit still depends on software
placement, scheduling, and an executable path. The next pressure is therefore
not another piece of hardware. It is the software required to use the machine.

## Software Is Part of the Machine

Hardware does nothing useful without the compilers, runtimes, libraries, and
applications that map a workload onto it. That dependency can fail in two
directions. A mechanism no compiler can target buys nothing, and a decision
made against a software stack that later changes may buy less than the
comparison predicted. The first problem concerns whether an executable path
exists. The second concerns whether the path remains representative while the
hardware is being built and after it ships.

### Executable Software Paths

Even when a hardware candidate clears physical constraints and evaluation
budgets, software must still be able to use it. The executable software path
includes the programming model or front end, compiler, libraries and kernels,
runtime, driver or firmware, operating system, and deployment controls needed
to use a hardware mechanism without losing its benefit to data movement or
overhead. Historical shifts like RISC and CUDA succeeded because they provided
the compiler support and programming models needed to make the hardware
accessible. Conversely, a design with high peak floating-point operations per
second (FLOPS) can fail if its software contract is unusable.
The IBM/Sony/Toshiba Cell Broadband Engine required developers to manage local
static random-access memory (SRAM) stores through explicit direct memory access
(DMA) transfers [@KahleEtAl2005Cell]. The mechanism makes the software
obligation concrete. A comparison must include the code, scheduling, and data
movement needed to use the local stores, not only the hardware's peak
throughput. Specialization without a usable software path carries costs that
peak hardware metrics do not show.

A hardware proposal is therefore incomplete until architects can inspect and test the software path needed to use it, and modern tensor programs make that path a search problem of its own. Frameworks like Halide and MLIR make scheduling, lowering, and intermediate representations part of the performance comparison [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM; @LattnerEtAl2020MLIR]. A hardware optimizer might select a mechanism that the compiler cannot target, or whose software overhead erases the predicted gain. A credible comparison must cover an executable hardware-software path, not a hardware block in isolation.

A joint search can, in principle, vary compiler schedules alongside hardware
parameters, using a shared schema such as an MLIR dialect to co-generate the
intermediate representation and the RTL. Such a search may find combinations
that separate hardware and software studies miss, but that is a hypothesis to
test rather than a guaranteed benefit. The software side has already
demonstrated search at enormous scale. Autotuners search billions of
tensor-program schedules [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. The stronger claim, that
hardware and schedule were co-optimized together to produce a better system,
still depends on an evaluation that can score both sides at matched fidelity.
That evaluation, not merely the search, is where co-design efforts stall.

At the distributed scale, this path becomes even more complex. It is not enough
to compile code for a single node. The path includes communication primitives
such as the Message Passing Interface (MPI) and NVIDIA Collective
Communications Library (NCCL), along with systems that coordinate computation
across many accelerators. Alpa automatically derives inter- and intra-operator
parallel execution plans for distributed deep learning, while Megatron-LM
combines tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism for large-model training
[@ZhengEtAl2022Alpa; @NarayananEtAl2021Megatron]. Collective selection,
topology awareness, and runtime scheduling can determine whether thousands of
accelerators deliver the throughput predicted for one device.

The instruction set architecture (ISA) is therefore only one boundary in a
larger software path. A new vector or accelerator interface must preserve the
relevant application binary interface, memory model, operating-system
assumptions, compiler lowering, runtime behavior, and compatibility tests. The
compiled program must also show that data movement and software overhead
preserve the predicted benefit. A design that cannot be compiled, scheduled,
and tested should not advance because a hardware proxy looks favorable.
Establishing one executable path does not freeze it for the life of the
hardware. For many modern comparisons, the limiting work is not proposing one
more hardware mechanism. It is re-establishing an executable, representative
comparison when the compiler, runtime, libraries, workload, or deployment
policy changes. The path can change while the hardware is still being designed.

### Software Change Can Invalidate Hardware Comparisons {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

Software and workloads can change while hardware is being designed. A
comparison can therefore become stale before the hardware ships, even when the
hardware itself has not changed.

Several parts of the target can move during that interval. AI models, precision
formats, sparsity patterns, compiler passes, kernel libraries, runtimes, serving
systems, batching strategies, fleet policies, and benchmarks can all change.
Precision formats
such as 8-bit floating point (FP8), 4-bit integer (INT4), and block-scale
formats[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02] may change even though supported data types
must eventually be fixed in hardware. Sparsity patterns, the structured or
unstructured zeros in weights or activations that hardware can skip, can change
as models and software evolve.
When a long-lived hardware decision still rests on an outdated workload, the
evidence no longer supports the original commitment.

[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02]: **Block-scale formats**: Low-precision number formats amortize shared exponent or scale metadata across a block of elements rather than storing independent metadata for every element [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. Committing to one in silicon fixes datapath choices while formats and workloads can continue to change, so the architect must judge whether the choice will remain useful.

The target moves in two different periods, and a useful comparison has to say
which one it covers. Before release, hardware and software teams can revise the
design together, although late changes become increasingly expensive. After
release the hardware is fixed, but compilers, kernels, libraries, runtimes, and
deployment policies keep improving, and that improvement changes performance the
initial evaluation never captured. A claim about post-release gains needs paired
hardware, workload, and software versions, as developed in
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, and it needs the architect to separate
improvements made for this hardware from unrelated change in the workload. The
first strengthens the case for the existing design; the second makes its
original evidence stale.

The hard part is deciding whether a change invalidates the architectural
comparison or leaves it intact. Detecting that two traces or software versions
differ does not answer that question. The architect must identify which differences
could reverse the decision and which measurements would test that possibility.

Specialization can improve efficiency while making a design less tolerant of
workload drift. Generality preserves flexibility, often at a cost in
performance per watt. The architect should therefore bound the workload, measure how
it changes, and revisit the hardware decision when its original assumptions no
longer hold.

One bounded example comes from AI workloads, where model scale and computation
can change visibly. Convolutional inference with fixed shapes can be regular,
while many autoregressive Transformer deployments add dynamic behavior through
growing key-value caches [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention], variable sequence
lengths, sparse
mixture-of-experts[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02] routing, or separate prefill and
decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. These are common sources of
changing memory behavior rather than a property of every model. An Epoch AI
report estimated roughly four- to
fivefold annual growth in training compute for recent notable and frontier
models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]. The separate fit in
@fig-training-compute-growth uses the displayed records from a frozen July 19,
2026 snapshot of Epoch AI's model database [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. Its roughly
4.4-fold rate is this chapter's fit to that snapshot, not a restatement of the
report. Both results depend on model class, outliers, and the form of the fit.
Compute growth is not itself
workload drift. It does show why evidence tied to one model scale, software
stack, or training regime cannot be transferred to another without checking
the assumptions. A useful comparison therefore states which model, compiler,
runtime, benchmark, trace, and deployment versions support each decision.

[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02]: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: A sparsely gated model activates only a subset of its expert subnetworks for each input [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE]. Input-dependent routing can therefore make the memory traffic a design must serve vary from token to token instead of following one fixed schedule.

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-compute-growth
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **This chapter's fit to the displayed database snapshot yields about 4.4-fold annual growth in training compute.** Each point comes from a frozen July 19, 2026 snapshot of Epoch AI's model database [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. The red line is a least-squares fit over the 2010--2026 records shown; it is separate from Epoch AI's reported 4--5-fold analysis through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]. The fitted rate describes this displayed snapshot rather than a universal rate, and it does not measure how changes in model scale overlap a hardware design program.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale scatter of AI training compute in FLOP versus publication date from 2010 to 2026. Points rise from about ten to the fifteenth FLOP in 2010 to over ten to the twenty-sixth by 2025, frontier models tracing the upper edge. A fitted line marks roughly 4.4-fold growth per year. AlexNet, AlphaGo Zero, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are labeled along the rising frontier."

import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: Epoch AI "Notable AI Models" database, restricted to models carrying a
# publication date and a training-compute (FLOP) estimate. Values are
# dataset-transcribed, not recomputed; the growth factor is this chapter's
# least-squares log-linear fit to the displayed snapshot (2010-2026)
# [@EpochAI2025AIModels].
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-training-compute.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2013.2, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2016.0), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor")

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
    p = by_name.get(key)
    if p:
        ax.annotate(label, (p["yr"], p["flop"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                    fontsize=5.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["muted"], lw=0.45))

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2010, 2026.7)
ax.set_ylim(1e14, 3e27)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Training compute (FLOP)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_spine].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.13, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

Across the horizontal date axis, the hollow notable-model records and filled
frontier records rise by orders of magnitude on the logarithmic compute axis.
The fitted line summarizes that cloud as more than fourfold annual growth. The
fit does not establish a universal rate, and a larger model is not automatically
a different workload. It supplies a bounded example of how model scale and the
software stack can change while a hardware project is underway. The model a
comparison was sized against may therefore differ from the model that eventually
runs, which is why the versions behind the comparison have to be recorded rather
than assumed.

Product announcements provide a visible interval between releases, but that
interval is not the period during which an architecture decision is exposed to
software change. The two product lines in @fig-apple-silicon-cadence illustrate
only how much announcement intervals can differ.

```{python}
#| label: fig-apple-silicon-cadence
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Announcement intervals do not establish architecture or AI effects.** Apple's M-series intervals shorten from 19 to 7 months while NVIDIA's data-center GPUs hold a roughly two-year cycle in the period shown [@Apple2020M1; @Apple2022M2; @Apple2023M3; @Apple2024M4; @NVIDIA2020A100; @NVIDIA2022H100; @NVIDIA2024B100]. Labels give the month gap between consecutive announced parts. The dates establish release timing only; they do not measure software change, development duration, per-generation architecture contribution, or a causal effect from AI assistance.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-row timeline. Apple's M1 (Nov 2020), M2 (Jun 2022), M3 (Oct 2023), and M4 (May 2024) fall 19, then 16, then 7 months apart, a shrinking interval; NVIDIA's A100 (May 2020), H100 (Mar 2022), and B100 (Mar 2024) fall 22 and 24 months apart."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

# Release dates transcribed from public product announcements (as fractional
# year); month gaps computed between consecutive parts. Same data as the prior
# static figure, restyled to the house chart family. As-of: 2026-07-19.
apply_style()

apple = {
    "y": 1.0, "color": COLORS["workload"], "ink": COLORS["workload_ink"],
    "label": "Apple Silicon",
    "pts": [("M1", "Nov 2020", 2020.83), ("M2", "Jun 2022", 2022.42),
            ("M3", "Oct 2023", 2023.75), ("M4", "May 2024", 2024.33)],
    "gaps": ["19 mo", "16 mo", "7 mo"],
}
nvidia = {
    "y": 0.0, "color": COLORS["designspace"], "ink": COLORS["designspace_ink"],
    "label": "NVIDIA datacenter",
    "pts": [("A100", "May 2020", 2020.33), ("H100", "Mar 2022", 2022.17),
            ("B100", "Mar 2024", 2024.17)],
    "gaps": ["22 mo", "24 mo"],
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.3, 2.35))
for s in (apple, nvidia):
    xs = [p[2] for p in s["pts"]]
    y = s["y"]
    ax.plot([xs[0], xs[-1]], [y, y], color=s["color"], linewidth=1.8, zorder=1,
            solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.scatter(xs, [y] * len(xs), s=42, marker="o", facecolor=s["color"],
               edgecolor=s["color"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
    for name, date, x in s["pts"]:
        ax.text(x, y + 0.30, name, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6,
                fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"])
        ax.text(x, y + 0.155, date, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.6,
                color=COLORS["muted"])
    for i, gap in enumerate(s["gaps"]):
        xm = (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2
        ax.text(xm, y - 0.135, gap, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=5.8,
                fontweight="bold", color=s["ink"])
    ax.text(2018.7, y, s["label"], ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.8,
            fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.set_xlim(2018.6, 2025.3)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 1.85)
for sp in ax.spines.values():
    sp.set_visible(False)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks([])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.98, bottom=0.04)
```

In the upper row, Apple's gaps shrink from 19 to 16 to 7 months. The lower row
holds near two years, at 22 and 24 months, for NVIDIA's data-center GPUs. These
observed intervals come from announcement dates. They do not bound a silicon
program or identify when an architecture choice became hard to change. Neither
sequence measures software change, ranks release strategies, isolates an
architecture contribution, or supports a claim that AI caused a release to
arrive sooner. The model-scale and announcement plots therefore do not
establish a design-cycle mismatch. They show why a comparison must record its
actual hardware, workload, and software exposure rather than infer it from a
release date.

Benchmarks are one way to keep a changing workload comparable. MLPerf defines
shared tasks and reporting rules for machine-learning systems
[@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. Within the same benchmark version, division, scenario,
and accuracy target, its inference rules make results from different systems
meaningfully comparable [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference] while leaving
submitters room to optimize their software toolchains
[@ReddiEtAl2021VisionBehindMLPerf]. That comparability is maintained rather
than inherent. It holds only while the community maintains the tasks and run
rules that make results comparable.[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]
When those rules change, an earlier comparison may no longer answer the same
question.

[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]: **Metrological traceability**: A measurement result is traceable when it can be related to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty [@NIST2021MetrologicalTraceability]. Architecture benchmarks do not create this kind of calibration chain, but their tasks, run rules, and measurement procedures still need explicit versions so reviewers can tell when two results remain comparable.

For the Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) target, “XR” is still too broad
to define a workload because it combines sensing, perception, graphics,
display, interaction, latency, quality-of-experience, and energy constraints.
Even a benchmark such as XRBench does not decide which traces, model versions,
deadlines, input distributions, and quality targets matter for this design
[@KwonEtAl2023XRBench].

The workload description should therefore be a versioned input rather than a
fixed name. Versioned traces, benchmark rules, compiler and runtime assumptions,
and tool results allow reviewers to see whether a hardware claim still applies.
The architecture study also needs a trigger for repeating the comparison when
one of those inputs changes.

When the machine spans a data center, that software path also determines how
hardware, networks, and facility resources operate as one system.

## Warehouse-Scale Computing Extends the Architecture Problem

Warehouse scale brings the preceding hardware and software pressures into one
architecture problem. Server and accelerator choices matter through network
topology, collective communication, cluster scheduling, failure handling,
deployment policy, and facility power and cooling. The comparison must therefore
judge the delivered service and operating constraints of the whole system, not
the efficiency of a node in isolation.

Aggregate demand, availability targets, or service objectives can require many
nodes even when one request fits on a single package. The boundary of the
computer can then become the entire data center. Scale-out networks, coherent
device and memory interconnects such as CXL,[^fn-cxl-c02] and cluster software
make placement and resource sharing architectural questions. At this scale, we
enter the domain of warehouse-scale computing (WSC)
[@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. The architectural problem
expands to encompass heterogeneous servers, shared cooling infrastructure,
facility power, and cluster-level scheduling.

[^fn-cxl-c02]: **Compute Express Link (CXL)**: A cache-coherent interconnect
standard for processors, accelerators, and memory devices. Its memory semantics
and switching support can make device-attached or pooled memory part of a
system-level provisioning decision [@CXLConsortium2026CXL].

Warehouse-scale systems are difficult to experiment with or simulate
efficiently, and component failure is a continuous condition rather than an
exceptional case [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Architects
therefore
combine trace-driven and discrete-event models, emulation, controlled
deployment, and production measurements. Every model and measurement leaves
something out. A trace may miss dynamic network congestion that creates
severe "tail at scale" latency [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale], while a node that
looks efficient in isolation can lose that benefit under stragglers or
distributed coordination. The difficulty is choosing evidence at a scale the
study can afford without reducing the system to a model that omits the behavior
under review.

Across these scales, the architecture comparison does not reset when the system
boundary expands. A core contributes policies and corner cases. An accelerator
adds workload mapping and a software interface. SoCs and chiplets add
integration, package, and test constraints. Wafer-scale and warehouse-scale
systems retain those obligations while adding repair, placement, networking,
failure handling, deployment, and facility limits (@fig-architecture-levers).

![**A wider system boundary accumulates comparison obligations:** A credible comparison carries forward the constraints, interfaces, software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives established at smaller scales while adding the obligations introduced by accelerators, package composition, wafer-scale fabrics, and warehouse-scale operation.](images/F2-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-alt="Five architecture scales run from core through accelerator, system-on-chip or chiplet, wafer-scale system, and warehouse-scale system. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path, which carries constraints, interfaces, workload and software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives into one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

The progression is cumulative, not a claim that every study must model an
entire data center. A core comparison may stop after microarchitecture and
physical checks. A warehouse-scale comparison cannot stop there because node
behavior reaches the service through software, networks, deployment policy,
and facility constraints. The appropriate boundary is the smallest one that
still contains the effects capable of reversing the decision.

Once hardware, software, network, and facility choices become part of one
comparison, the number of possible combinations grows faster than the capacity
to evaluate them.

## Design Spaces Grow Faster Than Evaluation Capacity {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Candidate-production capacity and evaluation capacity are different resources.
The layers above widen the set of designs a team can produce without increasing
the rate at which it can check them. The two quantities are easy to conflate
because only candidate production is easy to count.

Even a narrow comparison can contain many combinations, and the following
arithmetic is illustrative rather than measured. Suppose an architect explores
an accelerator and memory subsystem for one workload family and considers five
compute organizations, four vector or accelerator interface choices, six
memory hierarchy choices, four interconnect choices, three voltage/frequency
policies, and three compiler/runtime policies. The product is

```{python}
#| echo: false
toy_design_candidates = 5 * 4 * 6 * 4 * 3 * 3
toy_candidate_evaluations = toy_design_candidates * 3
```

$$
5 \times 4 \times 6 \times 4 \times 3 \times 3
$$
That is `{python} f"{toy_design_candidates:,}"` candidate configurations before
counting workload versions, process corners, thermal constraints, or reliability
cases. Checking each candidate at three fidelity levels would create
`{python} f"{toy_candidate_evaluations:,}"` candidate--evaluation combinations,
even before rejecting a single invalid design. Real architecture studies can grow far larger
or take far longer before silicon measurements are available.

The count alone says little about how many candidates can be evaluated well
enough to matter. If each surviving configuration needs an analytical model,
simulator run, synthesis check, or human review, a larger choice set also
increases the demand for feedback. Cheap models reduce evaluation cost, but
they do not establish whether a choice is legal or whether stronger
measurements will preserve its ranking. The practical limit is not how many
configurations an architecture study can enumerate. It is how many it can evaluate well
enough to support the next decision.



Other architecture tasks create similar problems in different ways
(@tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors). Mapping, design-space exploration (DSE),[^fn-dse-c02]
physical design, and software tuning do not share one measurement scale, but
each combines many possible choices with constraints that make only some of them
useful.

[^fn-dse-c02]: **Design-space exploration (DSE)**: The systematic search over a parameterized family of architectural configurations, such as cache capacities, issue widths, or accelerator array shapes, for the ones that best satisfy a stated objective under stated constraints. A trial may require a simulator run, analytical evaluation, synthesis run, or another architecture measurement, which is why the evaluation budget rather than the space size sets the practical limit.

Timeloop [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop], an analytical framework for mapping and
evaluating deep-neural-network (DNN) accelerators, provides a concrete lower
bound on this combinatorial growth. For a convolutional neural network (CNN)
layer with seven nested loops and a four-level memory hierarchy, loop ordering
and level-bypass choices alone produce $(7!)^4 \times (2^4)^3$ arrangements.
The first factor permits a different ordering of the seven loops at each of four
memory levels. The second permits a binary bypass choice at those four levels
for each of three data spaces. Factorization choices enlarge the mapspace
further. The formula is therefore not the complete count and not a count of
useful mappings. It isolates two sources of growth before legality, capacity,
and performance constraints remove most candidates.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| TPU-block floorplanning | The AlphaChip paper reported reducing placement generation from months of human effort to hours of machine time [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Routed physical quality and strong baselines still require separate evaluation. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |

: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[25,36,28]"}

The rows expose different parts of the same problem. Timeloop and MAESTRO show
how quickly mapping and accelerator choices multiply. AutoTVM shows that the
software schedule can create a large search space even after the hardware has
been chosen. The floorplanning example shows that producing a candidate quickly
does not establish its routed quality.

MAESTRO makes the distinction especially
clear. At 0.17M designs per second, its full 480M-candidate space can be examined
in under an hour. Cheap analytical feedback is plentiful in that case. The
difficult decision is which apparent winners justify more expensive evaluation.
Placed on one logarithmic axis, the four anchors' candidate counts can be
compared without treating equal counts as equal amounts of evaluation work
(@fig-search-vs-eval-gap).

```{python}
#| label: fig-search-vs-eval-gap
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Architecture search spaces span many orders of magnitude.** The scale anchors appear on one log axis, from the toy SoC design-candidate count computed above to a lower bound on Timeloop's mapspace from loop-ordering and bypass choices [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop; @KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Filled markers are stated or computed counts; the hollow marker is AutoTVM's order-of-magnitude estimate. Candidate count does not measure evaluation cost or evidence strength.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale strip chart plotting four search-space sizes as points: a toy SoC design space with 4,320 candidate configurations, MAESTRO's 480 million candidates, AutoTVM's roughly one billion tensor programs, and a Timeloop loop-ordering and bypass lower bound of 2.6 times ten to the eighteenth arrangements."

from math import factorial

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Data provenance (all values transcribed or computed from this chapter's text):
# - Toy SoC design candidates: 5*4*6*4*3*3 = 4,320, computed earlier in this chapter.
# - MAESTRO accelerator DSE: 480M candidates, stated [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO].
# - AutoTVM tensor programs: "on the order of billions" per GPU operator, stated
#   qualitatively (order-of-magnitude, hollow marker) [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM].
# - Timeloop loop-ordering and bypass lower bound: (7!)^4 * (2^4)^3 ~= 2.6e18,
#   computed from the stated expression [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Values not
#   recomputed from sources.
# As-of: 2026-07-14.

toy_candidates = 5 * 4 * 6 * 4 * 3 * 3
timeloop_mapspace = factorial(7) ** 4 * (2**4) ** 3

rows = [
    {"label": "Toy SoC design candidates", "note": "computed in this chapter", "value": toy_candidates, "right": "$4.3\\times10^{3}$", "stated": True},
    {"label": "MAESTRO accelerator DSE", "note": "480M candidates, stated", "value": 4.8e8, "right": "$4.8\\times10^{8}$", "stated": True},
    {"label": "AutoTVM tensor programs", "note": "order of billions, approximate", "value": 1e9, "right": "$\\sim\\!10^{9}$", "stated": False},
    {"label": "Timeloop ordering + bypass lower bound", "note": "$(7!)^{4}\\times(2^{4})^{3}$, computed", "value": timeloop_mapspace, "right": "$2.6\\times10^{18}$", "stated": True},
]

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.95, 2.75))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.42, right=0.82, top=0.79, bottom=0.22)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(2e1, 4e19),
    xticks=[1e2, 1e5, 1e8, 1e11, 1e14, 1e17],
    xticklabels=["$10^{2}$", "$10^{5}$", "$10^{8}$", "$10^{11}$", "$10^{14}$", "$10^{17}$"],
    xlabel="search-space size (candidate configurations)",
)

for y, row in enumerate(rows):
    ax.axhline(y, color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.65, zorder=0)
    if row["stated"]:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["designspace"], edgecolor=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.86, y - 0.17, row["label"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(-0.86, y + 0.23, row["note"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(1.04, y, row["right"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.1, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["designspace_ink"], clip_on=False)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The toy count sits in the thousands,
MAESTRO and AutoTVM cluster near $10^9$, and Timeloop's computed lower bound
lies almost ten orders of magnitude farther right. AutoTVM's hollow marker
distinguishes its order-of-magnitude estimate from the stated or computed
counts. The full span is nearly fifteen orders of magnitude, but horizontal
position encodes only candidate count. It says nothing about the cost, fidelity,
or decision strength of one evaluation. The architect must decide which choices
are worth testing and how many reliable evaluations the architecture study can afford.

Search capacity and evaluation capacity are separate budgets. ArchGym shows why
exploration methods need fair, reproducible comparison under common
environments and sample budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. This book applies a
broader accounting rule: compare evaluation fidelity, tool cost, total compute,
and engineering effort rather than equalizing candidate count alone. A fast
estimator can increase the number of candidates receiving a score without
increasing the number receiving a check strong enough to support commitment.

An executable software path is necessary, but it does not establish how many
candidates can be checked strongly enough to support a decision. The next limit
is the capacity and fidelity of evaluation and verification.

## Evaluation and Verification Limit Progress

The pressures so far enlarge the comparison. The ones in this section bound it.
Physics decides what can be built, powered, and cooled, while a fixed design-program
budget and schedule decide how much can be checked before commitment. More
resources may expand the evaluation, but they do not remove a physical limit or
make the available time and money unbounded.

### Physical and Measurement Limits {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

Physical effects create two distinct problems for an architecture comparison. An early model may omit an effect that later overturns the ranking, and the measurement that would settle the question may cost too much to run on every candidate. A design that looks sound at an architectural abstraction can still fail on a thermal hotspot or severe IR drop, revealing that the comparison hid a consequential physical effect. Reliability narrows the space again. Soft errors, silicon aging such as Negative Bias Temperature Instability (NBTI) and Hot Carrier Injection (HCI), and process variation [@Borkar2005ReliableSystems] affect viability in domains such as automotive systems under ISO 26262 [@ISO2018Iso26262]. Relevant evidence may include fault injection, aging simulation, circuit and physical analysis, accelerated testing, and field data.

Data-movement estimates, for example, can reverse an early ranking based on
compute alone. Moving data through a memory hierarchy often costs far more
energy than arithmetic. Horowitz's widely used estimates quantify the
difference [@Horowitz2014Energy]. A compute-only comparison can therefore rank
the wrong design. The result also depends on where the data resides, how often
it moves, who schedules it, what locality is available, which precision is
acceptable, and what the software stack can express.

The gap between arithmetic and memory-access energy spans about four orders of
magnitude on one logarithmic scale (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale). In the cited 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer add costs a
fraction of a picojoule, an 8 KB SRAM access about two orders of magnitude
more, and an off-chip dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) access about four
orders of magnitude more. These
values are order-of-magnitude anchors, not predictions for a current process.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Rough Horowitz 45\ nm energy values show why architecture comparisons must represent locality, buffering, precision, scheduling, and memory hierarchy rather than counting arithmetic alone [@Horowitz2014Energy]. The values are transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors, including the source's 1.3--2.6\ nJ DRAM range, not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, SRAM accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, add_note_box, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv
rows = [
    {"display_label": "32b integer add", "display_note": "baseline arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 0.1, "energy_high_pj": 0.1, "right_label": "1$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b floating-point add", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 0.9, "energy_high_pj": 0.9, "right_label": "9$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b integer multiply", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 3.0, "energy_high_pj": 3.0, "right_label": "30$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "32b floating-point multiply", "display_note": "local arithmetic", "energy_low_pj": 4.0, "energy_high_pj": 4.0, "right_label": "40$\\times$", "color": COLORS["blue"]},
    {"display_label": "8 KB SRAM access", "display_note": "64b cache access", "energy_low_pj": 10, "energy_high_pj": 10, "right_label": "100$\\times$", "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"display_label": "32 KB SRAM access", "display_note": "64b cache access", "energy_low_pj": 20, "energy_high_pj": 20, "right_label": "200$\\times$", "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"display_label": "1 MB SRAM access", "display_note": "on-chip memory access", "energy_low_pj": 100, "energy_high_pj": 100, "right_label": "1000$\\times$", "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"display_label": "off-chip DRAM access", "display_note": "off-chip memory access", "energy_low_pj": 1300, "energy_high_pj": 2600, "right_label": "13k--26k$\\times$", "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.45))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.17)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)
add_note_box(fig, "Rough 45 nm values from Horowitz; use for orders of magnitude.", xywh=(0.14, 0.035, 0.72, 0.075), fontsize=5.5)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The rows progress from arithmetic through on-chip SRAM to
off-chip DRAM at the far right. The DRAM marker is a range rather than a point,
and the ratios on the right are relative to the 32-bit integer add. Advanced
nodes change these values, so the comparison supports an order-of-magnitude
locality argument rather than a current-node energy estimate. It does not
remove the requirement to model the memory hierarchy before candidates are
ranked.

A useful architecture-level decomposition is
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} =
E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} +
E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} +
E_{\mathrm{leakage}} .
$$
This is a decomposition, not a circuit-level energy model, and it carries a diminishing-returns lesson. Optimizing the compute term yields shrinking system-level returns once the unoptimized data-movement and leakage terms dominate the power budget. It helps an architect
check whether the comparison includes every major source of energy that could
change the decision. A candidate that reduces arithmetic but increases memory
movement, interconnect traffic, control overhead, or leakage may make the
system worse. Nothing requires memory energy to rise when compute energy falls,
but an optimization focused on one term can allow the others to grow enough to
exceed the baseline total (@fig-waterbed-effect). For example, a candidate might
reduce a multiply-accumulate (MAC) array's arithmetic energy while requiring the
network-on-chip (NoC) to move enough data across the die that wire energy and
routing congestion dominate. An early proxy can rank the compute-heavy design
first even though the candidate later proves physically infeasible.
