![**Lower compute energy can hide a worse system total.** The illustrative candidate reduces compute energy but increases memory and interconnect energy enough to exceed the baseline total. A comparison that omits data movement can therefore rank the worse of the two designs first. The bar heights show the relationship and are not measured energy breakdowns.](images/F2-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="85%" fig-alt="Bar chart comparing a baseline energy breakdown with an illustrative candidate whose lower compute energy is outweighed by higher memory and interconnect energy."}

The baseline and candidate in the figure differ in more than arithmetic. The
candidate lowers the compute term, but its added memory traffic and
communication raise the system total above the baseline. The numbers are
illustrative, but the reversal is the point. An early proxy can favor a design
that loses once the comparison includes the costs of moving data through the system. This is the proxy-mismatch failure that @sec-feedback-verification-trust treats directly.

Interconnect costs deserve the same attention as memory movement. On-chip
networks, package links, memory interfaces, collectives, and host-device
protocols limit what a design can sustain. Early logical synthesis and
architecture models use approximate interconnect estimates, while placement and
routing expose the actual topology, congestion, and parasitic delays
[@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. A highly
parallel accelerator can therefore score well in an early model and fail timing
or routing after physical implementation. The failure is not that early tools
ignore wires entirely. It is that an optimizer can exploit whatever the
inexpensive model leaves out.

Timing, placement, routing, IR drop, thermal behavior, power delivery, leakage,
signoff, and test may also overturn an architectural choice, so architects must
consider the relevant electronic design automation (EDA) and physical-design
constraints early. These checks
rely on stateful tools, and a repeated run can be invalid if stale constraints
or cached netlists survive from an earlier candidate.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces treats the tool isolation and
execution mechanics. Here the point is that a clean tool state is part of a
valid comparison. Power and thermal density can flag a dense accelerator
mapping as risky before implementation, even when its average power clears an
early limit.

Later IR-drop analysis [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] and thermal signoff can confirm or
clear that risk once a placed netlist and current profile exist. Thermal design
power (TDP), a target for sizing the cooling solution rather than a measure of
sustained draw, is not the only limit [@Intel2014QuarkThermalGuide]. A large
specialized vector unit can create a rapid current change
when many lanes become active, producing voltage droop that constrains safe
operation. Early physical estimates, workload-aware power models, and closer
coordination between microarchitecture and physical design can expose that risk
before final signoff.

::: {.callout-engineer-move title="Measure the active-frequency policy"}
**The expectation.** Adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores
raises peak floating-point throughput.

**Measurement hypothesis.** Sustained wide-vector execution may raise power and
power-delivery demand enough for a processor to reduce frequency. The policy
and magnitude are implementation-specific and must be measured on the processor
under review.

**The lesson.** Peak vector width does not determine application speed by
itself. The architect must measure the active-frequency policy and the mix of
vector and nonvector work on the processor being evaluated.
:::

Timing signoff evaluates multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with
process corners [@Cadence2021Tempus]. A design may clear one view and fail
another. Because physical-design tools use heuristic optimization, one failed
closure attempt may not reveal whether the candidate or the tool setup caused
the failure. Comparing constraints, seeds, and repeated outcomes helps separate
the two.

Design Rule Checks (DRC) add another physical constraint. Routing must satisfy
restricted design rules, including minimum wire and via spacing
[@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Moving one macro can create many violations,
and repairing one can change neighboring routes and expose others. An automated
flow that cannot interpret those markers leaves repeated cleanup and rerouting
work for the implementation team.

Artifact-producing flows add a traceability problem to each of these physical
constraints. If a high-level tool emits RTL and a physical-design tool reports a
thermal failure later, tracing that result to the design decision that caused it
can be difficult. A saved RTL or topology artifact can be rerun, which is why
the design team must preserve the emitted artifact, parameters, and tool state
rather than depend on recreating it.
Evaluating physical constraints also requires bridging the semantic gap between
high-level proposals and EDA formats such as LEF/DEF and Liberty timing
files.[^fn-lef-def-c02]

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In place-and-route flows, LEF carries abstract physical information used to place and connect blocks, while DEF carries the placed and routed state of a particular design [@Si2LEFDEF]. Liberty carries characterized cell models for timing, power, noise, and related behavior [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. These implementation formats expose details that a high-level architecture description does not contain.

Multifidelity methods combine many inexpensive estimates with
selected high-fidelity evaluations and retain the stronger model to check
accuracy, a strategy that runs across engineering optimization rather than
architecture alone [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Physical constraints
require the same care. If an early model omits timing, congestion, thermal
behavior, or data movement, the architect needs a better model before comparing
more candidates.

An inexpensive energy proxy can support early screening, but finalists need a
current power model before they can support a power or efficiency decision. The
same limitation applies to the quantity being optimized. A design can lead on
the figures a data sheet reports and still fall behind on the work a real
program does.

AMD's Bulldozer architecture, the later FX-9590 product, and the Zen transition
provide one example of the gap between easy-to-count specifications and
workload behavior [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer; @AMDFXQuickReference; @AMDZen].

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** AMD's Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011) grouped two integer cores behind a shared front-end and floating-point unit and pursued high clock frequencies. Core count and frequency were easy to advertise and compare. The shared structures traded some per-thread capacity for throughput.

**The gap.** Those figures did not describe how a workload used the machine. The shared structures could become limits when two threads competed for them, while raising clocks increased power. AMD's later FX-9590 quick-reference specification listed a 220\ W power rating.

**The lesson.** Rank a candidate on the metric its workload rewards, not the
number that is easiest to count. In silicon that gap is expensive to discover,
because it appears only after the design has shipped. AMD later introduced the
Zen microarchitecture with renewed emphasis on core performance and
efficiency.
:::

These physical constraints and reliability concerns define a large search
space, but no early model eliminates the need for the stronger physical tools
required by the final claim. An architect must know which lower-cost estimates
are suitable for screening and which checks can still overturn the ranking.

### Evaluation Capacity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Larger systems expose more candidate configurations, software states, physical
corners, and failure modes. A larger choice space therefore increases demand
for simulator runs, synthesis and physical-design tools, verification, and
expert review. Architects cannot run every candidate through every available
tool. These evaluations consume different mixtures of compute, licenses,
schedule, and human attention, and feedback becomes scarce when an architecture
study requires more of that work than the available people and tools can
provide.

Evaluation tools form a spectrum whose tiers can sit orders of magnitude apart
in throughput, cost, and setup time. Suppose a simulator sustains ten to one
hundred thousand instructions per second. In that design case, representing one
second of a workload retiring one billion instructions per second takes roughly
three to twenty-eight hours.
Emulation and FPGA prototypes can run faster, but require different hardware,
compilation, and bring-up costs. Actual rates depend on the model, workload,
host, tool, and platform. The budget question is therefore not only whether a
candidate can be measured, but which candidates earn an expensive tier.

Architects have long rationed expensive evaluation through abstraction and
sampling. SimPoint selects representative program regions
[@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], and SMARTS bounds the error of sampled simulation
[@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Analytical models, reduced workloads, and
multifidelity evaluation serve the same purpose at different levels. Each
trades some detail for capacity, so the architect must state what the cheaper
evaluation preserves and which candidates still require a stronger check.

The allocation decision is itself difficult. Generating or scoring another
candidate may be cheap, but an inaccurate screen can discard a useful design or
send a weak one into an expensive stage. The architect must decide which
inexpensive checks can reject a candidate safely, which uncertainties require
stronger tools, and which measurements are likely to change the decision.
Otherwise, faster generation adds more work to the design program's most
expensive stages.

Leading-edge chip-development costs show the scale of this constraint. Public
estimates vary and should not be treated as universal accounting rules. The
Semiconductor Industry Association reports that the cost of designing a
latest-node chip rose from about \$30M for a 65\ nm chip in 2006 to more than
\$540M for a 5\ nm chip in 2020, a greater than $18\times$ increase
[@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. A McKinsey analysis
gives a similar order of magnitude, estimating roughly \$175M for a 10\ nm
design, \$300M for a 7\ nm design, and \$540M for a 5\ nm design when validation,
IP qualification, and related development costs are included
[@BauerEtAl2020SemiconductorDesignManufacturing]. These estimates include more
than masks or wafers. They reflect architecture, design, validation,
verification, IP, tools, and engineering labor.

A respin adds fabrication, validation, and schedule cost before the team learns
whether the correction worked. Simulation, emulation, and signoff exist in part
to reduce the chance of paying for that iteration again.

### Verification Capacity

Verification faces an exponential state-space upper bound, although structure,
abstraction, and verification methods determine the work a verification effort actually
performs. Adding one state-holding bit doubles the number of encoded states, so
a design with $n$ such bits can encode as many as $2^n$ states. The reachable
subset is usually far smaller and depends on reset and next-state logic, which
is why verification does not amount to enumerating every encoded state.

No verification effort establishes every relevant property by enumerating all encoded
states; the $2^n$ upper bound makes that strategy infeasible. Teams instead
combine coverage goals, assertions, formal results, constrained-random testing,
regressions, unresolved-defect review, and engineering judgment. A flattening
bug-discovery curve is one input to the tapeout decision, not the decision rule
by itself. A flood of novel candidates asks the team to repeat substantial parts
of that work.

Architectural evaluation must therefore consider verification work alongside
Power, Performance, and Area (PPA). A speculative cache-coherence protocol
might offer a measured performance gain yet still be a poor choice if its
additional states and interactions cannot be checked within the design-program budget.

Formal verification and simulation address different parts of this problem.
Simulation exercises selected behaviors under selected stimuli. Formal methods
prove a stated property over all behaviors covered by the model and its
assumptions, but their capacity depends on the property, abstraction, and
sequential state. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches behavior only to a
chosen depth. Combinational equivalence checking avoids sequential state by
checking whether two combinational descriptions implement the same function.
Sequential protocols, liveness, and system interaction still require a
carefully chosen mix of formal and simulation methods
[@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The industry has described verification pressure for a quarter century. The
2001 ITRS Design chapter called verification "a bottleneck that has now reached
crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design], and the Semiconductor Research
Corporation's MAPT roadmap still lists a widening verification gap among the
transitions ahead [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. This history
makes verification a condition worth checking in any proposal to generate
architectural candidates faster. It does not establish that verification is
the limiting condition in every design program.

If a design team can produce new register-transfer level (RTL) candidates faster
than it can create properties, tests, coverage, and review for them, generation
speed does not improve the tapeout decision. This gap grounds the state-space
argument in the daily work of a hardware team.

Foster's summary of the 2022 Wilson Research Group functional-verification study
reports that demand for integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC verification engineers
grew nearly three times
as much as demand for design engineers from 2007 to 2022, about 146 percent
versus 50 percent (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). Mean peak staffing was
roughly one verification engineer per design engineer across most market
segments, processor projects reached ratios as high as five to one, and design
engineers spent 49 percent of their time on verification in 2022
[@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy].

These figures do not prove that every project is verification-limited. They do
show that every invalid candidate reaching these stages consumes compute and
scarce engineering time. Generated candidates are cheap only until they require
tools, verification, and expert review.

The staffing ratio suggests a pressure rather than a universal project
diagnosis. A team must still measure whether its own limit lies in property and
test creation, simulation capacity, failure diagnosis, coverage closure, formal
analysis, or expert review.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak demand for IC/ASIC verification engineers grew about 146 percent from 2007 to 2022 while demand for design engineers grew about 50 percent, a 6.2 versus 2.7 percent compound annual growth rate [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers have printed data labels in the published study figures; hollow 2022 markers are chart-read approximations constrained by the study's stated growth figures.
#| out-width: "78%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries). 2007-2020
# values have printed data labels; 2022 values are chart-read, constrained by
# the study's stated callouts of +50% design and +146% verification demand
# growth since 2007 (2.7% vs 6.2% CAGR).
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv
years = [2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022]
design = [7.8, 8.5, 10.5, 10.3, 11.7]
verif = [4.8, 8.4, 11.6, 11.4, 11.8]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], verif_idx[:-1], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
ax.scatter(years[:-1], design_idx[:-1], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
# 2022 values are chart-read approximations: draw them hollow
ax.scatter([years[-1]], [verif_idx[-1]], s=26, facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([years[-1]], [design_idx[-1]], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white",
           edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(2022.6, verif_idx[-1], "verification\nengineers (+146%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(2022.6, design_idx[-1], "design\nengineers (+50%)", va="center",
        fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(2006, 2023)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks([2007, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2022])
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel("mean peak demand vs. 2007", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The two lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors are indexed to their 2007
values, so they show relative growth rather than absolute staffing levels. The
verification line rises much faster. Filled markers through 2020 carry printed
data labels in the published figures, while the hollow 2022 endpoints are
chart-read approximations constrained by the published growth rates. The
staffing data do not establish a single cause for that difference, and they do
not identify the cause of any one project's difficulty. They do show that
checking designs has consumed a growing share of engineering capacity in the
surveyed projects. A generated candidate that reaches this stage is no longer
free to evaluate.

Hardware is unforgiving because a defect in shipped silicon is costly to address and never cleanly undone. The 1994 Pentium FDIV flaw shows why early checks matter, as a defect arising from five omitted lookup table entries [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision] led Intel to report a \$475M pretax charge for replacement and associated costs [@Intel1995PentiumCharge]. More recently, the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre] exposed microarchitectural side channels in speculative execution. Published evaluations report workload- and processor-dependent performance costs for transient-execution defenses [@CanellaEtAl2019Transient], while those defenses do not remove the underlying hardware mechanism. These episodes show how a hardware flaw becomes an expensive, long-lived liability after a design has shipped, one that replacement, support, or a software workaround can mitigate but not cleanly remove.

The Pentium charge reflects one escaped defect, but leading-edge development
raises the cost of commitment even when no public recall occurs. Arm's 2023
prospectus reports International Business Strategies (IBS) estimates of
\$249M for a 7\ nm chip and \$725M for a
2\ nm chip [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. These figures are estimates rather
than universal project prices. They show that high-fidelity evaluation and
physical implementation at the leading edge consume engineering budgets, not
only simulator cycles.

The composition of the 2\ nm estimate matters more to an architect than its
total. Software development, verification, and IP qualification together
account for 71 percent (@fig-design-cost-composition). The public source does
not separate those activities, so the figure keeps them together. The durable
point is that most of the estimated budget sits in the software and checking
work needed to make a chip usable and trustworthy, not merely in producing the
design artifact.

The ranking is older than the node that produced these numbers. The 2001 ITRS
Design chapter reported that software already accounted for 80 percent of
embedded-systems development cost [@ITRS2001Design], measured on a different
accounting boundary than the figure below and so not a point on the same trend.
It is another example of substantial software cost, not evidence of a
two-decade trend between compatible measurements.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-composition
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Published estimates rise from \$249M at 7\ nm to \$725M at 2\ nm, and most of the 2\ nm cost is software and checking work.** Arm's prospectus reports IBS estimates for both totals and states that software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71 percent of the 2\ nm estimate [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. It does not publish the composition of the 7\ nm estimate or divide the three combined 2\ nm activities.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal bars compare estimated chip design cost. The 7 nanometer bar reaches 249 million dollars and has no published composition. The 2 nanometer bar reaches 725 million dollars; 71 percent is labeled as the combined cost of software development, verification, and IP qualification, and 29 percent as other design cost."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Sourced constants: IBS estimates as reported in Arm's Form 424B4
# [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The filing reports only the combined 71 percent
# share for software development, verification, and IP qualification.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv
cost_7nm_musd = 249
cost_2nm_musd = 725
combined_share = 0.71
combined_2nm_musd = combined_share * cost_2nm_musd
other_2nm_musd = cost_2nm_musd - combined_2nm_musd

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 1.75))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.98, top=0.94, bottom=0.28)

ax.barh([1], [cost_7nm_musd], height=0.52, color=COLORS["grid"],
        edgecolor=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.8, hatch="//", zorder=3)
ax.barh([0], [combined_2nm_musd], height=0.52, color=COLORS["blue"],
        edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=3)
ax.barh([0], [other_2nm_musd], left=[combined_2nm_musd], height=0.52,
        color=COLORS["grid"], edgecolor=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.8,
        hatch="//", zorder=3)

ax.text(cost_7nm_musd / 2, 1, "$249M\ncomposition not stated",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color=COLORS["ink"], zorder=4)
ax.text(combined_2nm_musd / 2, 0,
        "$515M  |  71%\nsoftware + verification + IP qualification",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.2, color="white", zorder=4)
ax.text(combined_2nm_musd + other_2nm_musd / 2, 0,
        "$210M\n29% other",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.1, color=COLORS["ink"], zorder=4)

ax.set_xlim(0, 760)
ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 1.55)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1], ["2 nm", "7 nm"])
ax.set_xticks([0, 200, 400, 600, 725])
ax.set_xlabel("estimated IC design cost (USD millions)",
              fontsize=6.6, labelpad=2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6.5, length=0, pad=5)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The bar lengths show the estimate rising from \$249M at 7\ nm to
\$725M at 2\ nm. In the 2\ nm bar, the blue segment
combines software development, verification, and IP qualification because the
source reports only their combined 71 percent share. The hatched remainder is
not a separately measured activity, and the 7\ nm composition is not stated.
The figure therefore supports the cost and composition claims shown, not a
claim about which individual activity grew fastest.

These costs change what should count as improvement. Producing more candidates
is not useful if every survivor adds simulation, synthesis, physical-design,
verification, and reviewer work to an already full queue. When results arrive faster than experts can reconcile
them, review queues grow and the team cannot close the decision. The team
must turn scattered tool results into a comparison that reviewers can inspect
and a decision can use.

## Compounding Pressures Shift the Limiting Work {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

The preceding pressures interact rather than merely accumulate. Specialization
expands the choice set, each hardware choice creates software obligations,
software changes can make the workload description stale, and physical effects
can reverse the remaining rankings. Every surviving candidate then adds work
for simulation, implementation tools, verification, and expert review.

The coupling matters because improving one stage can move the limit somewhere
else. Faster candidate generation can fill an evaluation queue. Faster
simulation can produce more results than reviewers can reconcile. A more
accurate physical model can reveal that the available choices cannot meet the
target at all. Design-space size, evaluation capacity, and decision quality are
different quantities, and increasing the first does not necessarily improve
the other two.

A design team should therefore look for the work that controls progress without
assuming one universal bottleneck. Useful observations include the age and
size of simulation or verification queues, the fraction of candidates rejected
as illegal, the number of repeated tool runs, missing or changing inputs, and
the point at which results wait for expert judgment. These measures diagnose a
particular design program. An industry trend cannot establish its local
constraint.

The work an architecture study must settle and the work its tools and reviewers can examine
diverge as two lines (@fig-scissors-gap). The region between them matters
because a candidate sitting inside it has been generated but not evaluated well
enough to accept or reject. A design team can grow that region without noticing.
Candidate count alone does not distinguish a design that survived review from
one that never reached a reviewer.

Missing or stale information can create a reinforcing bottleneck. It admits
invalid choices, spends scarce evaluation on them, and overloads review with
the resulting conflicts. Delayed review then leaves the design team with still
less current information (@fig-bottleneck-causal-loop). Breaking the cycle
requires repairing the information or decision boundary, not merely generating
or evaluating faster.

![**A local bottleneck can reinforce itself.** Missing information admits invalid choices, which waste scarce evaluation and overload review; delayed review then worsens the information available for the next choice.](images/F2-bottleneck-causal-loop){#fig-bottleneck-causal-loop width="72%" fig-alt="Four-node reinforcing cycle connecting missing information, invalid choices, wasted evaluation, and overloaded review."}

The reinforcing mechanism can produce a capacity gap across a design program.
The causal loop explains why unresolved work is created, while the scissors
shows what happens when that work arrives faster than tools and reviewers can
complete it (@fig-scissors-gap).

![**Design work can outpace the capacity to examine it.** In this conceptual relationship, the two straight lines cross as design scope and result volume increase. The widening region beyond the crossing holds candidates that have been generated but never evaluated well enough to accept or reject.](images/F2-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="85%" fig-alt="Conceptual diverging-line diagram in which tool and reviewer capacity initially exceeds work awaiting evaluation. The straight lines cross as design scope and result volume increase, after which work awaiting evaluation rises faster and creates widening unsettled work."}

At the left of the figure, tool and reviewer capacity can absorb the work
arriving for evaluation. The red line then crosses the blue line as work
awaiting evaluation and review rises faster than the available capacity. The
shaded region after that crossover is unresolved work, not a measured backlog,
and the horizontal axis represents increasing design scope and result volume
rather than elapsed time. The straight lines are schematic. They do not assert
a measured rate or functional relationship. The search-space
examples show how quickly a design study can produce candidates, while the
verification-staffing data provide one measured example of the engineering
effort needed to check increasingly complex designs. Together, they make a
mismatch between arrivals and completion capacity plausible, but only local
observations can establish it for a design program.

The scissors in @fig-scissors-gap has a well-established ancestor. The 2001
International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors described a design
productivity gap in which available transistors grew faster than the ability to
design them meaningfully [@ITRS2001Design]. The industry
responded to that gap in part by raising abstraction, including RTL synthesis
and IP reuse, so that one engineer's decision could govern more transistors.
Two decades later the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and
Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) restated the same shortfall
in their Decadal Plan for Semiconductors, naming a design gap between what a
technology permits and what can be designed in reasonable time and calling for a
tenfold or greater step in design productivity, though they scoped that target to
analog and mixed-signal work rather than to the loop as a whole
[@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. That history sets the bar for what follows in this
book. AI assistance earns its place only when the design team can show which work it
changes without weakening the checks needed for the decision.

A growing evaluation or review queue makes one mismatch visible, but not every
constraint appears as a queue. An architecture study may lack a workload trace, package
constraint, or software model that would reverse the result. Its available
choices may exclude the interface or memory organization needed to meet the
target. The decisive tool may be too expensive to run broadly, or the results
may be complete but still require expert judgment. The useful question is not
which category names the whole effort. It is which work currently controls the
next architectural decision and which check must remain authoritative if that
work is accelerated.

This is also why the widening region in @fig-scissors-gap is conditional rather
than universal. Some design programs are limited by candidate production, some by
evaluation, some by verification, and some by missing information or an
infeasible design space. The figure becomes a local diagnosis only when design-program
measurements show that work awaiting evaluation or review is growing faster
than it is completed.

## Where AI Assistance Might Help {#sec-feedback-and-verification-become-the-bottleneck}

The chapter has exposed five recurring limits. They are scattered or stale
design context, scarce strong evaluation, a missing executable artifact, a
choice space larger than the evaluation budget, and limited tool or reviewer
attention. Assistance might reconcile context, screen work before an expensive
tool, construct an artifact, search the choice space, or reduce repeated tool
operation and triage. The relevant question is which limiting work the
assistance addresses in a particular architecture study.

Existing research supplies concrete examples. Models adapted to company design
collateral retrieve and organize information, while tool-using systems translate
requests into electronic design automation (EDA) commands
[@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. Predictive models and learned
physical estimators screen candidates before detailed simulation or analysis
[@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling;
@XieEtAl2020PowerNet]. Learned search heuristics guide accelerator exploration
[@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo], and generators can draft testbenches when
verification-authoring effort is the relevant limit [@QiuEtAl2024AutoBench].
At warehouse scale, learned schedulers and reconfigurable fabrics show how
automated decisions can be evaluated against cluster-level workloads and
system-level constraints [@MaoEtAl2016DeepRM; @JouppiEtAl2023TPUv4].

Software co-evolution creates another assistance target. A tool-using
regression system can ingest new compiler builds, rerun architecture
benchmarks, and report that a candidate's standing has changed. That system can
reduce manual reevaluation, but it cannot decide whether the change invalidates
the architecture comparison. The architect still has to judge which software
changes could reverse the decision.

Regression automation is one specific use of AI on the software side.
Amarasinghe's Compiler 2.0 proposal points to a broader opportunity. It
argues that multicore processors, vector instructions, accelerators, and
heterogeneous systems have returned more of the performance burden to software
developers, and calls for modernizing compilers through better abstractions,
machine learning, and other modern techniques
[@Amarasinghe2026Compiler20CSAIL]. Such assistance still has to produce an
executable path and demonstrate its benefit on the hardware and workloads under
review.

Each use has a different cost and a different failure mode. The comparison in
@tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound brings the five limits together and identifies
the check that must remain authoritative in each case. A method is useful only
when its reduced engineering work is worth the data, compute, tool calls, and
review it adds.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing fields or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and the architect's judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change the decision. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the first pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, authoritative tool verdicts, and expert review where required. |

: **Each use retains an independent check.** AI may reduce information
search, evaluation, artifact creation, design-space search, or tool-operation
work. It does not replace the provenance, calibration, engineering tools, or
architectural judgment that establishes the result.
{#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[20,29,23,28]"}

Several forms of assistance may address different work in the same design program.
Combining them does not make the result self-validating. If every component
depends on the same incomplete workload description or model, the complete
system can be internally consistent and wrong.

A useful comparison must therefore include the cost of assistance. Surrogates
need data from stronger tools. Generators can add candidates to a full
evaluation queue. Tool-using systems consume licenses, simulation time, and
review attention. The limiting work and the independent check determine whether
a particular use of assistance helps. Once those are known, the next question
is which method or combination fits the work, which
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops.

That test must also be allowed to reject AI assistance. AI is the wrong
intervention when an established deterministic method already solves the
limiting task within the required cost and time, a proposed learned method
lacks representative data, or no independent check commensurate with the
consequence is available. It is also a poor trade when inference, tool calls,
and added review cost more than the engineering work they save. The real
obstacle may instead be an infeasible requirement or a decision that faster
search cannot settle. In those cases, the right answer is a conventional
method, a change to the architecture problem, or no added automation.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**The system spans the stack.** The mobile extended-reality (XR) target requires a RISC-V software path, a
compute organization, memory and interconnect choices, a strict power envelope,
and verification across the resulting interfaces. No single method covers
that chain.

**Assistance has several roles.** A retrieval system can assemble the current workload, ISA, compiler, package,
and tool constraints. Predictors can screen microarchitecture and physical
risk. An optimizer can compare mappings and resource allocations, while
generators can draft RTL, compiler support, or tests. A tool-using system can
run simulators and implementation checks and return failures to the relevant
stage.

**Shared assumptions remain mandatory.** The Lighthouse example also shows the limit of this decomposition. Every
component must refer to the same workload, interfaces, and technology
assumptions. The selected design still needs executable software, stronger
physical analysis, and independent verification. Assistance can connect and
accelerate the work; it cannot turn an inconsistent set of local results into a
sound system design.
:::

The public AlphaChip debate illustrates the same boundary. Producing a macro
placement quickly and establishing its routed physical quality are different
claims. Comparisons of learned placement have depended on cases, compute
budgets, implementations, and downstream checks
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement;
@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. The technical disagreement is not resolved
here. Its lesson for this chapter is that candidate-production speed cannot
stand in for matched, downstream evaluation.

No single method diagnoses its own need, performs the work, and supplies the
independent check at the same time. The architect still owns the question,
scope, comparison, and decision.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

Modern architecture work creates research problems in diagnosing which work
controls progress, detecting where an intervention moves that pressure, and
allocating the costly evaluations that support a decision.

**Diagnosing compounding pressure.** Assistance should relieve the work that
limits a supported architecture decision rather than hide or relocate it.

- **How can an architecture team identify the work that currently limits its
  next decision?** The challenge is to infer the controlling constraint from
  records of ongoing architecture work and determine whether relieving it
  shortens the time to a supported decision.

- **How can an architecture team detect when AI assistance relieves one
  bottleneck but creates another?** Faster candidate construction or cheaper
  screening can increase later simulation, correction, verification, or
  review. Signals across the complete tool path must distinguish a genuine
  reduction in total work from a queue shift or delayed downstream cost.

**Detecting evaluation pressure.** Large design spaces matter only through the
measurements and checks that can distinguish useful candidates.

- **How can an architecture project detect that candidate production is
  outpacing evaluation and review?** Candidates follow different simulation,
  implementation, verification, and review paths whose costs change as the
  study narrows, so backlog growth alone does not identify a persistent capacity
  mismatch. The research problem is to determine when that imbalance will
  prevent a supported decision before the evaluation budget is consumed.

- **When does expanding a design space weaken rather than improve an
  architecture study?** Under fixed evaluation and review budgets, more
  candidates can expose a better design or spread credible evidence too thin.
  The open problem is to determine when additional choice improves the
  supported result and when it creates more weakly evaluated work.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Improve the work that limits the decision"}
As system complexity compounds, identify whether exploration, evaluation,
verification, or review limits the next supported architecture decision, and
reduce that work without moving the burden elsewhere. Count progress only when
the complete comparison still carries its workload, executable software path,
physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification.
:::


System complexity changes what a fair architecture comparison must carry.
Microarchitecture, specialization, system composition, evolving software,
physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification add coupled work rather
than independent concerns. A local improvement can move cost elsewhere in the
system or expose a constraint that an earlier model omitted.

The technology dividend has also changed. More transistors no longer produce
proportional frequency or single-thread performance automatically. Architects
must obtain more of the benefit through parallelism, specialization, software,
and composition, while the cost of evaluating and verifying those choices
continues to rise. A large design space matters only when the team can evaluate
enough of it, at sufficient fidelity, to change the pending architecture
decision.

That is why AI assistance is potentially useful. Retrieval can assemble
scattered context, predictors can ration expensive evaluation, generators can
draft artifacts, optimizers can search large spaces, and tool-using systems can
connect proposals to existing engineering checks. None of these roles is
universally helpful, and none makes its own output trustworthy.

The central lesson is to evaluate the complete architecture work. A hardware
claim inherits its workload, software path, physical assumptions, tool state,
and verification. Assistance earns a place when it improves that complete
comparison while preserving the measurements and checks that can reject a bad
design. Applying it well therefore requires a systematic way to organize
AI-assisted design work, which @sec-architecture-20-ontology takes up.
